slides.title: Light: Mirrors and Lenses
slides.subtitle: At a science centre, Meena looked into a row of curved mirrors — her face went huge, her brother turned upside down, and then she shrank to a tiny version of herself. Let us find out why.
points: Can we make mirrors which give enlarged or diminished images?
Why do vehicle side-view mirrors warn "Objects in mirror are closer than they appear"?
Why is there a curved line on some reading glasses?

slides.title: What are spherical mirrors?
slides.intro: Meena had used a plane mirror before, where the image was erect and the same size as her. The science centre's mirrors were curved inward or outward. What kind of mirrors are these?

slides.title: Look at yourself in a shiny spoon
slides.purpose: A curved surface is the simplest spherical mirror you own. We use a spoon to see **how a curved mirror differs** from the plane mirror you already know.
steps: Hold — bring the inner curved side of a shiny spoon close to your face
Notice — is the image different from one in a plane mirror?
Move — slowly take the spoon away and watch the image change
Flip — turn the spoon to its outer side and repeat
slides.observe: The **inner** (inward-curving) side shows your face **inverted**; the **outer** (outward-bulging) side shows it **erect but smaller**. A spoon acts like a mirror — and curved mirrors like this can be specially made.

slides.title: Mirrors shaped like part of a sphere
slides.body: Curved mirrors, like the spoon, can be specially made. **Spherical mirrors** are a common type of curved mirror, shaped like part of a **hollow glass sphere**. Mirrors whose reflecting surfaces are spherical are called **spherical mirrors**.

slides.title: Concave vs convex
slides.leftBody: Its reflecting surface curves **inwards** (like the inner spoon). In its schematic representation, the non-reflecting surface is shown shaded.
slides.rightBody: Its reflecting surface curves **outwards** (like the outer spoon). Again, the non-reflecting surface is drawn shaded in the representation.

slides.title: How a spherical mirror is really made
slides.body: A spherical mirror can be thought of as **part of an imaginary hollow sphere** — but it is not made by slicing one. It is made by grinding a flat glass piece into a curved surface. Coat the **outer** curved surface and you get a **concave** mirror; coat the **inner** surface and you get a **convex** mirror.

slides.title: Tell concave from convex
slides.purpose: Two unlabelled mirrors sit on the table. We want a quick way to **identify which is which** without touching the reflecting side.
steps: Place — set both mirrors with their reflecting surfaces facing upwards
View — bring your eye down to their level and look from the side
Identify — see whether each surface curves inwards or outwards
slides.observe: Seen edge-on, the **concave** mirror's surface dips **inwards** and the **convex** mirror's surface bulges **outwards** — that shape alone tells them apart.

slides.title: What are the characteristics of images formed by spherical mirrors?
slides.intro: Meena's face grew large in one mirror and her brother flipped upside down in another. Does the image depend on how far the object is from the mirror?

slides.title: Move a toy near and far from each mirror
slides.purpose: A spherical mirror's image changes with distance. We move one object and watch **how size and orientation change** in a concave and a convex mirror.
steps: Set up — stand a concave and a convex mirror upright, side by side
Near — place a small toy 3–4 cm in front; note its size and whether it is erect
Far — slowly move the toy away and watch both images change
Repeat — try each mirror on its own and record your observations
slides.observe: In the **concave** mirror the close toy is **erect and enlarged**; move it away and the image **inverts** and keeps shrinking. The **convex** mirror keeps the toy **erect and diminished** throughout. **Lateral inversion** is seen in all three types of mirror.

slides.title: From enlarged and erect to inverted
slides.body: Placed **close** to a concave mirror, the image is **erect and enlarged**. Move the object **farther** and the image becomes **inverted**; it is enlarged at first and then keeps getting smaller. This is why a **dentist's** concave mirror gives an enlarged view of teeth held close to it.

slides.title: Always erect, always smaller
slides.body: A convex mirror always forms an **erect** and **diminished** image, shrinking a little as the object moves away. Because it curves **outwards**, it shows a **much wider area** behind — which is why vehicle side-view mirrors are convex, and why such mirrors guard road bends and big stores.

slides.title: What are the laws of reflection?
slides.intro: We have seen images in plane, concave, and convex mirrors. But are there laws which govern how light bounces off a mirror in the first place?

slides.title: Shine a beam on a plane mirror
slides.purpose: Before we can state a law, we must measure. We send a thin beam onto a mirror at different angles to compare the **angle in with the angle out**.
steps: Slit — cover a comb with black paper, leaving one middle opening, to make a thin beam
Shine — using a torch, let the beam fall on an upright plane mirror on white paper
Trace — draw the incoming ray, the mirror, and the reflected ray on the paper
Measure — draw the normal at the point of incidence and measure both angles
slides.observe: Done carefully, the **angle of incidence (i) equals the angle of reflection (r)** every time. When the beam falls **along the normal**, both angles read **zero**.

slides.title: Incident ray, normal, reflected ray
steps: Incident ray — the ray of light that falls on the mirror
Normal — a line drawn at 90° to the mirror at the point of incidence, O
Reflected ray — the ray that comes back from the mirror
Angle of incidence (i) — between the normal and the incident ray; angle of reflection (r) — between the normal and the reflected ray

slides.title: Angle in equals angle out
slides.caption: Measured from the normal, the angle of incidence (i) equals the angle of reflection (r). When the ray falls along the normal, both angles are zero.

slides.title: Bend the paper under the reflected beam
slides.purpose: There is a **second** law of reflection, about which plane the rays lie in. We bend the paper carrying the reflected beam to test that idea.
steps: Extend — place a stiff chart-paper sheet so part of it juts beyond the table edge
Shine — send a beam onto the mirror and see the reflected beam on the extended flat part
Bend — fold the extended part down along the table edge and look for the beam
Flatten — straighten the paper again and observe
slides.observe: The reflected beam **disappears** when the sheet is bent and **returns** when flattened. So the incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray **all lie in the same plane** — the second law of reflection.

slides.title: What every mirror obeys
slides.body: **First law:** the angle of incidence (i) is equal to the angle of reflection (r). **Second law:** the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the **same plane**. These laws of reflection hold for **all** mirrors — plane, concave, and convex alike.

slides.title: Many parallel beams on curved mirrors
slides.purpose: Each ray still obeys the laws of reflection — yet a curved mirror does something a flat one cannot. We send **many parallel beams** at each mirror to see it.
steps: Slits — leave many openings of the comb uncovered to make multiple parallel beams
Plane — let the beams fall on a plane mirror and watch the reflected beams
Concave — repeat with a concave mirror
Convex — repeat with a convex mirror
slides.observe: A **plane** mirror keeps the reflected beams **parallel**. A **concave** mirror brings them together — they **converge**. A **convex** mirror spreads them apart — they **diverge**. The curved surface does this even though each ray follows the laws of reflection.

slides.title: Converge or diverge
slides.body: Each ray obeys the laws of reflection, but the **shape** of the mirror takes over for a parallel beam. A **concave** mirror makes parallel rays **converge** to a point; a **convex** mirror makes them **diverge**. The curve, not the law, decides which.

slides.title: Burn paper with a concave mirror
slides.purpose: If a concave mirror converges sunlight, the rays gather at one spot. We test whether that **concentrated light** carries enough heat to burn paper. **Safety first:** do this under adult supervision; never look at the Sun or into the mirror, and aim the spot only at paper.
steps: Hold — face a concave mirror's reflecting surface to the Sun, over a sheet of newspaper
Adjust — change the distance until you get a sharp, bright spot on the paper
Steady — hold both still for a few minutes
Watch — see whether the paper begins to char and smoke
slides.observe: Sunlight reflected by the mirror **concentrates** on that bright spot, producing enough **heat to ignite** the paper. The same idea drives **solar concentrators** and **solar furnaces** — hot enough even to melt steel.

slides.title: What is a lens?
slides.intro: Curved mirrors reflect light. But what happens when light passes through a transparent material whose surface is curved, instead of bouncing off it?

slides.title: Read text through a water drop
slides.purpose: A simple curved surface can change what you see through it. We make a tiny dome of water and check **how it changes text** seen beneath it.
steps: Coat — rub a thin film of oil or wax onto a flat glass or plastic strip
Drop — place a small drop of water on the coated spot so it stays nicely rounded
Examine — note that the drop's surface is curved outward
Look — slide printed text under the drop and look straight down through it
slides.observe: The text under the **outward-curved** drop looks **enlarged** — the drop acts like a simple lens, just as a **magnifying glass** does. A **lens** is a piece of transparent material with curved surfaces; like mirrors, lenses can be convex or concave.

slides.title: Convex vs concave lens
slides.leftBody: **Thicker at the middle** than at the edges. A water drop or magnifying glass works this way, making print look bigger.
slides.rightBody: **Thicker at the edges** than at the middle. Unlike mirrors, lenses let light pass **through** them, so we see things **through** a lens rather than in it.

slides.title: View an object through each lens
slides.purpose: Like a concave mirror, a convex lens changes its image with distance. We move an object behind each lens to **compare what we see**.
steps: Set up — stand a convex lens upright in a holder, object behind it at lens level
Near — look through from the other side; note the image when the object is close
Far — slowly move the object away and watch how the image changes
Repeat — do the same with a concave lens and compare
slides.observe: Behind a **convex** lens the close object looks **erect and enlarged**; moved away it becomes **inverted**, enlarged at first then **diminished**. Behind a **concave** lens the object is **always erect and diminished**, shrinking as it moves away.

slides.title: Parallel beams through glass and lenses
slides.purpose: Just like curved mirrors, lenses can bend a parallel beam. We pass **multiple parallel beams** through a flat glass plate and through each lens to compare.
steps: Stand — fix a thin glass plate or lens upright between two books, paper spread on each
Glass — let multiple parallel beams fall on the thin glass plate and watch them emerge
Convex — repeat with a convex lens
Concave — repeat with a concave lens, then record your observations
slides.observe: The beam passes **straight through** the flat glass. A **convex** lens makes the beams **converge**, so it is a **converging lens**; a **concave** lens makes them **diverge**, so it is a **diverging lens**.

slides.title: Lenses everywhere
slides.body: A **convex (converging) lens** is also able to burn paper, since it converges sunlight just like a concave mirror. Lenses are everywhere — **eyeglasses, cameras, telescopes, and microscopes** all use them, and even your **eye** holds a convex lens that **changes its shape** so you can read or look far away.

slides.title: The chapter in a nutshell
slides.body: A **concave mirror** can enlarge, diminish, or keep size the same, and its image may be erect or inverted; a **convex mirror** is always erect and diminished. The laws of reflection hold for all mirrors. A concave mirror and a **convex lens converge** light; a convex mirror and a **concave lens diverge** it.

slides.title: Words to carry forward
slides.body: The vocabulary of mirrors and lenses from this chapter:

slides.title: Keep the curiosity alive
slides.subtitle: From a puzzling spoon to dentists' mirrors, solar furnaces, and the lens in your own eye — the same laws of reflection and the same curved surfaces shape all of it. Keep observing.
